title: Redwood throughput tuning - technical deep dive
summary: SE-led deep dive on throughput tuning for latency-sensitive customer workload. Discussed continuous batching, scheduler parameters (max_num_seqs, max_tokens), tokenization distribution, prefix/KV caching strategy, and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed on next steps: run 2-week benchmark with Canary profile, share config suggestions and cost/latency spreadsheet, and schedule follow-up pilot kickoff.
transcript:
[00:00] Alice (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give control to Ben for the deep dive. We have about an hour, is that still ok?
[00:10] Mei (Head of ML): Yep, sounds good. We really want to focus on throughput; our latency SLO is 150ms p95 and cost needs to stay under, uh, $0.5 per 1k tokens - approximate.
[00:24] Ben (SE): Great, thanks Mei. Quick agenda: 1) workload profile 2) continuous batching overview and scheduler knobs 3) KV cache approach 4) quantization & token limits 5) recommended config and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:35] Carlos: Yes, please. I'll share screen with our traffic histo— small correction, our median request length is 18 tokens but we have tails up to 1,200 tokens for long summaries. Most calls are chat-like, so short-medium.
[00:48] Ben: Perfect. So continuous batching is one of the big wins for throughput when you have variable arrival rates. The basic idea is we keep a short window and always try to batch while respecting latency SLOs. Key knobs are max_num_seqs (how many concurrent sequences in a batch), max_tokens or max_total_tokens, and the scheduler's wait budget.
[01:05] Dana: Quick question — how does Redwood handle very long tails? If someone submits 1,200 tokens it can blow out batch shapes.
[01:12] Ben: Right. Two strategies: 1) cap per-request tokens with graceful truncation or downstream chunking, and 2) isolate long requests to a separate priority queue — we call this long-running or streaming lane, it gets its own scheduler pool so it doesn't block short requests. You can set max_num_seqs lower on the long lane.
[01:30] Carlos: So practically what would you set for our traffic? Our RPS is about 45 at peak and burst to 120 for 10–20s during reports.
[01:39] Ben: For that profile we'd start with a standard host config: max_num_seqs=16 for the short lane, max_total_tokens=4096 per batch, and scheduler wait budget of 8–12ms. That aims to hit high GPU utilization without bumping p95. If p95 creeps up we dial down max_num_seqs.
[01:55] Mei: Where does continuous batching get tricky? I mean I've seen in other runtimes that you can degenerate latency when request sizes vary.
[02:03] Ben: Exactly. The degenerate case is when the batch waits for a large request and short ones sit idle. Our scheduler uses size-aware packing: it'll pack sequences sorted by token length, with small ones grouped together so they don't wait behind large sequences. Also we have dynamic deadline scheduling: if a request is near its latency deadline it gets boosted.
[02:22] Dana: Are there knobs for the deadline boosting? We have strict p95 so we'd tune that.
[02:27] Ben: Yes — two parameters: latency_deadline_ms (how long a request can be delayed before priority) and boost_threshold (percentile to consider boosting). Default is 100ms and 90th percentile boost; you can lower for tighter SLOs.
[02:40] Carlos: What about KV cache behavior? We do a lot of conversational turn-taking — reusing KV caches could help, right?
[02:47] Ben: Totally. KV cache gives big speedups for multi-turn chats because past tokens don't get recomputed. On Redwood we keep KV per-session with an LRU eviction and you can pin sessions for VIP customers. Important memory knob is max_kv_size per GPU — if you overcommit you'll evict more aggressively. For your workload, pinning session keys for 10% of high-value users plus a shared prefix cache should help a lot.
[03:10] Mei: Any gotchas with private deployment/VPC? We plan to run Private in GCP.
[03:16] Ben: The runtime is the same, but network latency to the control plane (for metrics and rollouts) and the storage latency for KV checkpointing matter. For Private we recommend colocating KV store (Redis or Rocks) in the same VPC subnet, and using local SSDs for model cache. Also check that HSM/KMS latency doesn't add to token generation if you do per-request key fetches.
[03:37] Dana: For quantization — we want to reduce cost but need to avoid quality regressions. What are your recommendations?
[03:44] Ben: We usually use 4-bit quantization for embeddings/encoder-heavy models and 8-bit or mixed for large generative models, paired with small eval sets. Redwood Optimize will run a quantization recommendation and rank configs by latency and quality regression. For production I recommend staged rollout: canary with 5% traffic, compare eval metrics and human review.
[04:05] Carlos: Back to scheduler knobs: you mentioned max_num_seqs, but what about max_tokens_per_seq or per-batch token budget?
[04:12] Ben: max_tokens_per_seq is enforced to avoid pathological memory spikes. We recommend setting it slightly above your observed 99th percentile. Per-batch budget (max_total_tokens) limits the maximum matrix sizes and keeps latency predictable. For example with a 32GB A100, a safe per-batch token budget for your model is ~12k tokens total. We'll provide an exact table for your model.
[04:38] Mei: Can we run a benchmark with our real traffic? We want to see p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens across configs.
[04:45] Ben: Yes — recommended approach: 1) export a 24–72h anonymized trace with arrival times and token lengths; 2) we'll replay it through Redwood's benchmark runner with: baseline (no batching), continuous batching default, and tuned config (max_num_seqs=16, wait_budget=10ms, kv_pinning). We'll return latencies, throughput, and estimated cost.
[05:04] Carlos: How invasive is the agent/replay? We can't send PII.
[05:09] Ben: Only timings and token lengths are needed; replace any payload text or use hashed tokens. We'll provide a script.
[05:16] Alice (AE): We'll attach the benchmark spreadsheet and the config template to the CRM after the call.
[05:20] Dana: On failure modes, what happens if GPU memory spikes — do requests get dropped or queued?
[05:25] Ben: We have graceful backpressure: the scheduler will reject new low-priority requests when memory pressure is too high (you can configure rejection policy to 429 or 503), and critical requests go to a fallback model (smaller quantized variant). We also recommend autoscaling burst capacity for spike protection.
[05:43] Mei: For our numbers — you suggested max_num_seqs=16. If we want lower latency at cost of throughput, we reduce to 8?
[05:50] Ben: Correct. Lower max_num_seqs reduces batching queuing latency; throughput per GPU drops though. It's a tradeoff curve we'll plot in the benchmark.
[05:57] Carlos: Any quick wins we can try on our side before the benchmark?
[06:01] Ben: Yes. 1) enforce client-side max prompt size for interactive routes, 2) enable session KV for chat clients, 3) use token-aware batching hints in the SDK (we've added opt-in hints to avoid long-short blocking).
[06:15] Mei: Ok great. Can you also share the recommended quantization profiles for our model, and the rollout checklist?
[06:20] Ben: We'll share the Optimize report and a rollout checklist doc — canary config, eval prompts, rollback steps.
[06:27] Alice: Let's summarize next steps.
[06:29] Ben: I'll take ownership of the benchmark run once you send the anonymized trace. We'll also share a tuning doc and a spreadsheet with cost/latency estimates.
[06:36] Carlos: When can you start?
[06:38] Ben: As soon as you send the trace — ideally this week. We'll aim to return initial results in 10 business days.
[06:44] Dana: Perfect. Thanks all.
[06:47] Mei: Thanks Ben, Alice.
[06:49] Alice: We'll follow up with the docs and a time for pilot kickoff.
[06:54] [END]
